clue.text: Nicking old motorbike in Oxfordshire town

parts.note: nicking a cup or plate is chipping it
Norton is a classic British motorcycle make

explanation.surface: Someone pinches a vintage motorbike somewhere in an Oxfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nicking' looks like British slang for stealing, but here it means making small cuts. CHIPPING NORTON is a market town in the Cotswolds.
explanation.definitionFit: Chipping Norton is a real market town located in the county of Oxfordshire, so this is a straightforward place-name definition.

clue.text: Where can Ethel and I set off a firework?

indicators.note: to set off is to start something going or explode it, so the letters are blown apart and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about where two people might safely let off a firework.
explanation.walkthrough: The question reads like a request for a bonfire-night venue; the whole of its first half is the letter supply.
explanation.definitionFit: A Catherine wheel is a spinning firework pinned to a post, named after the wheel of Saint Catherine's martyrdom.

clue.text: Fashionable butler's beginning to grass? Keep it in the family!

parts.note: what is fashionable is in

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is only its opening letter, so just that one is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of butler
a reed is a tall grass of wet places

explanation.surface: A grand household whose butler starts off its matchmaking, keeping marriages within the family.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation turns the definition into a cheeky imperative: mate only with relatives.
explanation.definitionFit: To inbreed is to mate closely related animals or people, literally keeping reproduction within one bloodline.

clue.text: I left Capitol vaguely concerned with public affairs

indicators.note: something rendered vaguely is not set out precisely, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who walked out of the US Capitol building, dimly interested in government business.
explanation.definitionFit: Political describes matters of government and the state, the business conducted on behalf of the public.

clue.text: Points to turbulent river, getting more jittery

parts.note: north and east are compass points

indicators.note: turbulent water churns and swirls, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone directed towards a raging river grows increasingly anxious.
explanation.walkthrough: Points of the compass supply two letters; any pair can work, and the crossings or anagram settle which.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervier is the comparative of nervy, meaning anxious and on edge, so it means having greater nerves.

clue.text: Doctor R. Mount's patent medicine

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so these letters are falsified into another arrangement

parts.note: the initial and surname, possessive s included

explanation.surface: A physician named R. Mount sells his own branded cure.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor reads as a title on a name but works as a verb meaning tamper with.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a quack remedy sold under its maker's claims, exactly a proprietary patent medicine of dubious value.

clue.text: Sportsmen take this course at university

parts.note: a run is a course or route, as in a ski run
in British usage a student is up at university

explanation.surface: Athletes taking a course of study while at university.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain one goes up to university and is up while in residence. A bowler in cricket or a long jumper takes a run-up before delivering.
explanation.definitionFit: Bowlers, jumpers and javelin throwers all take a preliminary sprint before their action, which is called the run-up.

clue.text: Exposed to vile stormy weather

parts.note: a secret that is exposed is out

indicators.note: a stormy sea is tossed about, so these letters are thrown into another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone left out in horrible stormy weather.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weather' looks like a noun completing the storm picture; it is the verb meaning come through or survive.
explanation.definitionFit: To weather a crisis is to come through it and survive, and to outlive something is likewise to last beyond it.

clue.text: Gallic footballers introducing new style of pants

parts.note: Gallic means French, from Gaul

indicators.note: introducing something means bringing it inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: footballers kick the ball
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A French football team launching a new design of trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: In British English pants are underpants, not trousers; French knickers are loose, wide-legged women's underwear.
explanation.definitionFit: French knickers are a particular cut of loose women's underwear, and pants is the British word for underwear.

clue.text: Members of constabulary set out in columns

indicators.note: members are parts of a whole, so a run of letters is taken from within the following word

parts.note: the middle letters of this word

explanation.surface: Police officers lined up in ranks and files.
explanation.definitionFit: Tabular data is arranged as a table, laid out in rows and columns for easy reading.

clue.text: US politician's near to breaking

indicators.note: breaking something smashes it to pieces, which can then be rebuilt differently

parts.note: the final letter of the possessive plus the two words after it

explanation.surface: An American politician is on the verge of cracking under pressure.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks like part of the definition, but its S belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A senator is an elected member of the United States Senate, the upper chamber of Congress.

clue.text: Permission to leave former husband before tea break

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: break means smash apart, so these letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks to leave an ex-husband before the afternoon tea break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tea break' reads as one phrase but splits into fodder and signal. An exeat is the permission a British boarding school gives a pupil to go away briefly.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeat is Latin for 'let him go out', the formal leave of absence granted by a college or boarding school.

clue.text: Bursting in, one runs ahead into trouble

parts.note: Roman numeral one

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the word just before is stirred into a new order

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for a run, doubled for the plural
a team that is ahead is up
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone charging into a room, racing ahead straight into difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into trouble' reads as a phrase but is fodder plus signal. Doubling a letter for a plural, as pp for pages, gives RR for runs.
explanation.definitionFit: An irruption is a sudden violent entry or invasion, a forcible bursting into a place.

clue.text: Drunk on cider, Mother loses her head: it's unseemly behaviour

indicators.note: someone drunk is all over the place, so the words that follow are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: losing a head means the opening letter is cut off

parts.note: Mum is the British word for mother

explanation.surface: Mum gets tipsy on cider and forgets herself, behaving disgracefully.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum without her first letter leaves UM, which follows the rearranged cider phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecorum is a lack of propriety or good manners, conduct that offends against what is fitting.

clue.text: Saucy, but salt-free

definitions.meaning: second meaning: of water, not salty

explanation.walkthrough: 'Saucy' and 'salt' both point to the kitchen, suggesting seasoning; one sense is cheekiness, the other water that is not sea water.
explanation.definitionFit: Fresh can mean cheekily forward, as in getting fresh, and fresh water contains no salt.

clue.text: Giveaway contains empty page

parts.note: an empty seat is a free one
a sheet of paper is a page

explanation.surface: A free gift turns out to be nothing but a blank sheet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' looks like a container signal, but the two pieces simply sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A freesheet is a newspaper handed out at no charge, so it is a giveaway publication.

clue.text: Calm liberal making a stand

parts.note: to calm fears is to ease them
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A cool-headed Liberal politician takes a firm position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making a stand' sounds like taking a principled stance; the stand is a physical frame.
explanation.definitionFit: An easel is a wooden frame that holds a painter's canvas or a display board upright.

clue.text: Think spouse is seething quietly inside

indicators.note: inside tells us one piece sits within the other
seething water bubbles and churns, so the preceding word is stirred up

parts.note: taken as written
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Someone suspects their husband or wife is silently furious.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppose is to assume or believe something is probably so, which is one sense of think.

clue.text: Clergyman cruelly abused prisoner

indicators.note: treating something cruelly mangles it, so the following word is twisted out of shape

parts.note: taken as written
a con is a convict

explanation.surface: A priest has viciously mistreated an inmate.
explanation.definitionFit: A subdeacon is a minor cleric ranking below a deacon, so he is a member of the clergy.

clue.text: Des and Pete about to get soaked

indicators.note: about can mean around in all directions, so the letters are moved round

parts.note: the two names, with the joining word dropped

explanation.surface: Two friends are on the point of getting drenched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of'; split it into the signal and a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Something steeped has been left to soak in liquid, like tea leaves in hot water.

clue.text: Promise to marry Yankee writer

parts.note: a Yankee is a British accumulator bet on four horses
Philip Roth, the American novelist

explanation.surface: Someone pledges to wed an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yankee writer' looks like one American author; in British bookmaking a Yankee is an 11-bet wager on four selections.
explanation.definitionFit: To betroth is to pledge someone formally in marriage, an engagement promise of a future wedding.

clue.text: Tory has strong support

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative
firm means solid and strong

explanation.surface: A Conservative politician enjoys solid backing.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: To confirm a claim is to back it up or corroborate it, giving it support.

clue.text: Believe box can be found in bottom draw

parts.note: to hope something is to trust or believe it will be so
a chest is a large box

explanation.surface: Someone trusts that a box will turn up in the lowest drawer.
explanation.walkthrough: A bottom drawer, printed here as 'draw', is the British name for the linen and household goods a woman collects for marriage; Americans call it a hope chest.
explanation.definitionFit: The American hope chest and the British bottom drawer are the same thing, a store of items gathered before marriage.

clue.text: Some Armagnac or gin is Palace favourite

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so just part of the following words is taken

parts.note: letters spanning the end of the brandy, the middle word and the start of the spirit

explanation.surface: A nip of brandy or gin is the favoured drink at Buckingham Palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Queen Elizabeth II was famous for her corgis, the short-legged Welsh dogs kept at Buckingham Palace.
explanation.definitionFit: The corgi was the royal family's best-known pet breed, so it is a favourite animal of the Palace.

clue.text: Initially sort of nervous in Concorde, travelling at the speed of sound

definitions.text: travelling at the speed of sound

indicators.note: initially points to the start of each word, so only opening letters are kept

parts.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A slightly anxious passenger aboard the supersonic airliner Concorde.
explanation.definitionFit: Sonic relates to sound waves, and a sonic speed is one equal to the speed sound travels.

clue.text: She finally acquired cleavage — it increases self-esteem!

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word, so only its closing letter is kept

parts.note: the closing letter of she
to have acquired something is to have got it
a cleavage is a split or division, as a rip is

explanation.surface: A woman who has just had a bust enhancement feels much more confident.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleavage' suggests a neckline; it is used in its other sense of a split or tear.
explanation.definitionFit: An ego trip is an activity pursued chiefly to boost one's own sense of importance and self-regard.

clue.text: Former cardinal gets jail term

parts.note: one is a cardinal number
a prisoner gets time, a term in jail

explanation.surface: An ex-cardinal of the Church is sent to prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' suggests a churchman; it means a counting number.
explanation.definitionFit: One-time means having been so in the past, as in a one-time champion, which is a former one.

clue.text: Old-fashioned ass takes a Murdoch paper

parts.note: in American slang ass is the backside, a behind
The Times of London is owned by Rupert Murdoch's News UK

explanation.surface: A foolish fogey takes his daily copy of a Murdoch newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ass' looks like a fool, but here it is the bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To be behind the times is an idiom for lagging behind current fashions or ideas, being out of date.
